title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores $19.5 Million in Huge Second Weekend, ‘Clayface’ Leads With $24 Million Debut
description: Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-b
body:
Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office.

	Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “Clayface” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” was surprisingly close after defying box office expectations again. The stranger-than-fiction film collected a spectacular $19.5 million while expanding to 2,655 venues in its sophomore outing.
	

	Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are 28% above its launch of $15.6 million from 855 theaters, which marked the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years. So far, the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed movie has earned a remarkable $45.1 million domestically to date. After capturing the zeitgeist and selling out screenings across the country, awards sages are predicting it could become the first documentary to ever score a best picture nomination at the Oscars.


	“Clayface” arrived on the lower end of the studio’s expectations of $25 million to $35 million. The antihero adaptation earned another $19 million overseas from 76 markets for a global tally of $43 million. Along with a positive reception, the film seems well-positioned theatrically because it cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a way smaller budget compared to DC’s other recent tentpoles, including this July’s “Supergirl” and 2025’s “Superman.” Although “Superman” was a decent hit with $618 million against a $225 million budget, “Supergirl” was a setback for the newly relaunched comic book studio after bombing with $126 million against a $170 million budget. DC wanted to keep costs low on “Clayface” because it’s a body-horror thriller that’s much darker than those family friendly adventures. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Audiences enjoyed the film, which holds an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.
	

	“Over the years, there have been a dozen spinoffs of superhero villains and antiheroes, from ‘Joker’ to ‘Venom’ to ‘Kraven the Hunter,'” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This picture was wisely conceived as something different, costing a fraction of what those films cost, and it should be profitable when it finishes all ancillary business.”

	“Clayface” opened alongside a smattering of new releases, including Laika’s stop-motion animated “Wildwood,” Black Bear’s offbeat romantic comedy “Wicker” and Sony’s literary adaptation “Klara and the Sun,” starring Jenna Ortega.

	“Wildwood” debuted at No. 3 with $11 million from 2,718 venues, landing above projections of $6 million to $8 million. It’s a promising start for original animation, which has been challenged in the years following the pandemic. And “Wildwood” has the benefit of sterling reviews (a rare 100% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (an “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), which should help the film stick around beyond its opening weekend. However, this movie carries a hefty $100 million price tag (stop-motion animation is labor intensive and takes years to produce) and likely won’t turn a theatrical profit. 

	“This is a very good opening for a new animated film from outside of the studio development and distribution system,” says Gross. “Audiences love this movie, but it needs a very long run to recoup its costs.” 

	So far, “Wildwood” collected just $3 million internationally from 11 markets. The movie hails from Laika Studios, best known for making the 2009 stop-motion fantasy “Coraline.” This is the company’s first release since 2019’s “Missing Link,” which opened to $6 million from 3,413 theaters and ended its run with $26 million globally. “Wildwood” was directed by Laika’s CEO Travis Knight and revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. 

	“Wicker” captured fifth place with $6 million from 1,471 locations, a strong start for the low-budget film. Black Bear acquired the well-reviewed movie after Sundance for $2.5 million. Olivia Colman stars as an ostracized woman who commissions a local basketmaker to weave her a husband. Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy in the village. 
	

	“Klara and the Sun” collapsed at No. 15 with $720,000 from 880 locations. Sony scaled back the theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as “calamitous” and “confoundingly awful.” Luckily the Taika Waititi-directed adaptation for a modest $20 million, so inevitable box office losses for the studio won’t be too painful. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, “Klara and the Sun” takes place in the dystopian future as an obsolete companion android (Ortega) tries to bond with her new owner, a young sick girl named Josie.

	More to come…

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores $19.5 Million in Huge Second Weekend, ‘Clayface’ Leads With $24 Million Debut

title: ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale
description:
“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” ends on a far more hopeful note than Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo’s original 1971 trial.

	Th
body:
“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” ends on a far more hopeful note than Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo’s original 1971 trial.

	The first iteration of the Stanford prison experiment took 24 white male college students (save one Asian American) and paid them $15 a day to participate in a two-week simulated prison environment in order to study the effects of incarceration. Students were randomly assigned to the roles of guards or inmates, with the guards pressured to maintain order by any means necessary. Participants fell into their roles a little too well and, after a prisoner rebellion, increasingly cruel forms of punishment from the guards and a number of students suffering mental breakdowns, the experiment was ended on the sixth day. It’s widely considered one of the most notorious, ethically compromised psychological studies in history.
	

	And so, on Oct. 21, Netflix debuted “The New Stanford Prison Experiment,” a six-episode reality-TV version from executive producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth (“Top Chef”) that saw thirty entrants of various racial, geographical and economic backgrounds — including three women — partake in a two-week simulated prison environment, only this time in the decommissioned cell block of an actual working prison. Eight of them were assigned as guards, working in two separate shifts, and the other 22 prisoners. Unlike the 1971 version, the show implemented safeguards to ensure safety, including background checks and psychological testing for all involved; informed consent; medics, psychologists and off-duty guards on call 24/7; a safe word (“pineapple”) if participants ever felt they needed to leave or talk to a therapist and/or producer; and conducted regular interviews with participants throughout. There was also a team of three experts on hand observing the proceedings: Alison Wood Brooks, a behavioral scientist who teaches at Harvard Business School; Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist; and Michael Cantrell, a former federal corrections officer.
	



	Over the course of the experiment, five people bow out — the first of whom, Larry Foy, a former convict who goes by the nickname “Scary Larry,” gets severely triggered by being in a prison environment again and demands to be removed. “Nobody thought it would affect him in the way that it did, but we knew he could make the decision for himself and relieve himself of the experiment if it became too much, which he in fact did,” Lipsitz explains to Variety. “I think he was surprised by how much it affected him.”

	The experiment nearly unravels by day six (again) when two prisoners, Pete and Brandon, are placed in “23 and 1” for conspiring against the guards, meaning they must remain locked in their cell for 23 hours and a day and are given 1 hour a day outside it for showering and recreation. Brandon nearly bails, but decides to stay after an emotional phone call with his mother. “We thought it would end on the same day that the original experiment did,” admits Lipsitz, adding that the Pete and Brandon predicament raises an interesting question for audiences: “Do you see them as ridiculous pains in the ass or antiheroes?”

	To complicate matters further, four “phases” were implemented by producers: Transformation, Hierarchy, Role-Reversal and Self-Governance. During the Role-Reversal phase, the most punished inmates — Pete and Brandon among them — are made guards while the most power-obsessed guards, such as Chet Hudson, an oil rigger from Mississippi who put Pete and Brandon in “23 and 1,” and Chris Lee, a 41-year-old startup CEO with a more kumbaya approach, are converted to inmates. Chet, uncomfortable with being power-less, quits after a day; meanwhile, the inmates who’d been fed up with Pete and Brandon for their mischief-making in their previous role begin crowding the duo and come perilously close to attacking them when the three female guards from the other shift intervene to stop it. They’re led by Laura Berens, a CEO and entrepreneur, who emerges as the finest leader of the experiment with her firm-but-fair methods.

	“As a woman running the show, it was important to reflect the female experience as well and look at that in terms of power dynamics,” offers Lipsitz. “I think that Laura really emerged as the strongest leader of the whole series when they’d ended their shift and checked on them to see how it was going to go. It was almost motherly concern. They did not want a prison riot.”
	



	

					Laura Berens has the guards’ attention in “The Stanford Prison Experiment.” 
									Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026
	



	As for that hopeful ending, during the final “Self-Governance” phase, all of the rules are thrown out the window and the prisoners are allowed to do as they please. Though some inmates demand to stay and finish the experiment, including Lee, he’s convinced by a fellow prisoner, the Black comedian Mike Paramore, that it would be far more powerful if all the prisoners walked out of the facility together arm-in-arm, suggesting an image of racial unity. And that’s what they do, ending the experiment on the thirteenth day.

	“We felt it was really powerful and did not see that coming at all,” says Lipsitz. “I would hesitate to come to any conclusions about race and gender, but I think it holds up a mirror to a lot of those issues and is very revealing,” Cutforth remarks. “It’s something me and Jane are particularly proud of and felt privileged to be able to make the show.”

	“One really fascinating thing about it is, there’s a lot of talk about the manosphere and the ‘male loneliness epidemic,’ and having those men together with no phones, alcohol or women, these men from all different backgrounds really bonded in an amazing way,” Lipsitz adds. “There were conversations in there where you could hear that they’d learned from each other and were fascinated by other people’s POVs — people they would have never come across in society except for here. It seemed like a very positive experience for them, and for the women as well.”

	Will there be a second season of “The New Stanford Prison Experiment?” Lipsitz and Cutforth hope so.

	“I would love to have the opportunity to do it again, for sure,” shares Cutforth. “That prison setting is an incredible petri dish, and I would love to see more things play out there.”

	“Obviously, we couldn’t do it the same way,” says Lipstiz. “I think it would be interesting to do it with women and ask some different questions or frame it differently. But we’re really proud of it and hope people watch, debate and think about what it means in modern society. That’s the most you can ask for.”

schema.headline: ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale

title: ESPN Taps Marvel’s Vision to Boost ElClásico’s Debut on ABC
description:
The Vision, the Marvel super-hero, must tackle two important missions on Sunday.

	Not only does the character have a new streaming series on Disne
body:
The Vision, the Marvel super-hero, must tackle two important missions on Sunday.

	Not only does the character have a new streaming series on Disney+ that needs promotion, but he’s been tapped by Disney sibling ESPN to lend some pizzazz to Sunday’s telecast of ElClásico, the fierce soccer match-up between Barcelona and Real Madrid, which is being broadcast on ABC for the first time.

	In a bid to get more people interested in the event, ESPN and Marvel Studios devised an intriguing collaboration that will include a 30-second promo voiced by Paul Bettany, the actor who has long played Vision in various Marvel films.  A Q&A with the actor focused on soccer, has been distributed across ESPN’s FC social platforms, and a “motion poster” dropped on ESPN FC’s Instagram and TikTok Stories, as well as ESPN Deportes’ Instagram Story.
	



	During pre-game coverage Sunday, a custom promo is scheduled to air in both ESPN’s English-language and Spanish-language coverage. ESPN FC’s X and Facebook accounts will share that vignette ahead of the match.


	Other parts of the Disney empire were also tapped. “Live with Kelly and Mark” promoted the match during the week, as did several of ESPN’s studio program, including “SportsCenter.” ESPN also enlisted creators Devin Caherly and Dylan Acanfora to create content from Barcelona.

	The event’s broadcast television debut in the U.S. starts 4 p.m. eastern on Sunday, October 2. Soccer greats including Lamine Yamal, Pedri, Kylian Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Vinícius Júnior are expected to play. The telecast will also be available on ESPN+, ESPN Deportes and the ESPN App.

schema.headline: ESPN Taps Marvel’s Vision to Boost ElClásico’s Debut on ABC

title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins Explains That [SPOILER] Cameo, Introducing Gotham City to the DC Universe and All the Shape-Shifting Kills
description:

body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Clayface,” now playing in theaters.

	Batman fans will have to wait patiently for the next installment in Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s Caped Crusader saga, but they can get a peek at the rebooted DC Universe’s Gotham City in “Clayface.”

	“Clayface” is an R-rated body horror that follows the shape-shifting Batman foe. It blends a supervillain origin story with some stomach-churning scares and comes from horror veterans including director James Watkins and a story by Mike Flanagan. Tom Rhys Harries plays Matt Hagen, an A-list actor who is brutally disfigured by a gangster. With his face ripped up and his career destroyed, Matt turns to an experimental procedure from Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), which heals him — but slowly turns him into a clay-covered monster.
	

	Matt’s blood cells gain the ability to transform and instantly reshape his body into someone else, such as Corr or the gangster who disfigured him or even his own father (played in a quick cameo by Aaron Paul). He loses control of his own body and sanity as these newfound shape-shifting powers help him enact bloody revenge on the mob who ruined his life. In the end, Matt kills everybody who wronged him (plus several innocent people), and is forced to live as a reclusive mud monster in the sewers.


	Clayface has appeared in many Batman comics through the years, and he’s a classic villain who’s made the crossover into animated shows and video games. This version of him has also technically already appeared in the rebooted DC Universe in James Gunn’s animated series “Creature Commandos,” but now the monster gets his own origin story and live-action debut. The movie also gives the first look at Batman’s hometown of Gotham City in the new DC Universe. Gunn’s “Superman” kicked things off in Metropolis last year, but now another one of DC’s most famous cities gets unveiled in “Clayface.”
	

	With Variety, Watkins explains finding the final Clayface monster look, recruiting Paul for his cameo and creating Gotham City.



	

									©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	The Clayface name has been used by several villains in Batman comics. How did you land on the Matt Hagen version instead of the first iteration, Basil Karlo?

	It was really landed by Mike Flanagan and the script. I read all of them, Basil Karlo and all, afterward because there are bits and bobs that are kind of cherry-picked from all over the place. But the key journey, and that’s what Mike had chosen, was the Matt Hagen version. If you’d have gone with Basil Karlo, it’s a little bit too gothic or too hard to do in such a modern idiom. The Matt Hagen is a more relatable version. Whether it’s Basil Karlo and Boris Karloff, there are all those characters that it’s referring back to in the Golden Age of Hollywood, that sort of thing. This is something that can sit in our contemporary time. Our Gotham is not entirely contemporary. It slightly steals from a few different genres. We wanted it to be slightly timeless, but it can play as contemporary.

	This is the first time we’re seeing Gotham in the rebooted DC Universe. Did you have a specific year or time you wanted to set the world in?

	We deliberately wanted it to be a bit muddy. James Price, our brilliant production designer, and I talked a lot about creating the sense of the world, and we wanted it to feel like a character in the movie. We wanted this oppressive world where the buildings really dominate. We looked at a lot of 1930s German expressionist cinema with huge dominant buildings and the odd angles and the noir-ish shadows. We also looked at street photography from New York from the ’70s, the ’80s and the ’90s. It was all before New York had been cleaned up. The lighting is different. It’s a lot of neon. There’s a lot of practical lighting. There’s a lot of dirt and eccentricity on the street. We wanted to definitely frame Gotham as a contrast to Coast City, with the colors, the bright sunshine, the sky, the sea. You see verdant greens and textures and stuff like that, which you don’t really see in Gotham. You barely see the sky, and it’s a very heavy atmosphere.

	There are so many face-swapping scares in the movie. How many of them were practical camera tricks vs. special effects?
	

	A lot of it is in camera. The scene in the nightclub where he comes in and he’s on this dark, lethal, vengeful journey, I wanted to give the audience permission to enjoy his payback before it goes too far. There’s a lot of in-camera wipes. We did so much stuff old-school. He takes somebody out, then he goes past a pillar, then I knew that I’d use that pillar as a wipe, then I do the scene again with another actor and they’d come out of the pillar or Tom would come out of the pillar. It was really good fun.

	Did you have a contortionist for the nightclub scene too?

	My guiding thing is if I can do it practically, I will try and do it practically. So after that fall down the stairs, which is a stunt with two stunt people, then they’re all on the floor, we were like, “Well, should we try it with a contortionist?” for that sense of bodies out of shape. If you can do it in camera, why not, right?

	That sequence also has a quick cameo from Aaron Paul, who plays Matt’s dad in one of his transformations. How did you get him to shoot that scene?

	It was like, “Who can we get to play Matt’s dad?” And I really, really love Aaron Paul as an actor. I know it’s tiny, but I think he was living in Paris, and so somebody said, “Why don’t we reach out?” He’s such a nice man, and he came in and was just a really good sport and a really fine actor. It’s a tiny moment, and it’s a sort of really an Easter egg, isn’t it? But the idea that Matt’s not his father and sort of thing. It was a pleasure to meet him. He was like, “Yeah, cool DC movie. I’ll show my face for a moment.” It was very nice of him.

	How did you decide on the final look for the Clayface monster?

	I took everything as a reference and tried to choose, because there are so many versions in the comics. We did about 19 different iterations. You want to honor the comics, but at the same time, you want to make sure it can work as live-action because it’s obviously a different medium. The key thing for me was making sure that it captured the emotion, the man inside the monster. I was particularly obsessed with his left eye and the pain and the heartbreak within that and the scream, the quality of his voice. I first responded in Mike’s script to the idea of the tragedy and the journey of his character and where he ends up and going with him.
	

	It was an awful lot of work and tiny tweaks. Where one fold of flesh goes makes such a difference. It’s sort of unquantifiable, but you just have to look at it and something about that feels good and real. It was a lot of work, but it was fun.

	How did you pull off the suffocation scene where Matt kills his friend, Corey, by pulling him into his body?

	The actual pulling into the body is practical with augmentation, but he is wearing a rig on his body with a big cavity in it so he could pull Josh [James], who plays Corey, into his chest. It’s like his face in the airplane. That is prosthetic makeup, not VFX. There’s a tactile quality that just reads when it’s on camera, that I think is very hard to replicate.

	So the airplane scene, where he has to cut the strips of clay between his eyes with scissors, is mostly practical?

	He had contact lenses, and then he had prosthetic makeup on. He actually had five pairs of scissors. We had sharp ones, blunt ones, rubber ones, one with a green screen tip, one without a tip. It was all on a gimbal, so the bathroom could move in real time and create the jolts. I was on the microphone talking everyone through the scene and jolts and Tom’s reactions. Tom figured out a way to — it sounds awful — where he could shove it in slightly above his eye, but the way it reads on camera, you can’t tell. He was quite in control and safe. For the close-ups, we had an eyeball, which was enormous, with a massive pair of scissors.

	How many different facial prosthetics did you have for Tom to wear?

	We had so many stages. I can’t say how many prosthetics, but we had like 65 stages at one point. That was all with bandages and this and that, but there was an awful lot because there were subtle differences between different melts and droops, and some that can have a pulley that you could tug. Obviously, some of these things you can augment with VFX because Tom can’t literally do that. But always having that base layer again gives you something that has a sort of heft to it.

	I kept looking for a bat flying around or some kind of reference to Batman, but there isn’t anything overt. Did you ever plan to include more Easter eggs in the movie?

	I actually think there are lots of Easter eggs that I probably don’t even know about because the graphics department was always throwing in posters and stuff. What I really responded to was the fact that it was a standalone story, and so for me to read that and then to try and get too cute or crowbar something in that wasn’t merited to the narrative felt gimmicky, I suppose. There was zero pressure to do it. I signed up to a certain story, which I believed in, and I just tried to tell that to the best of my abilities.
	

	After the movie ends, do you have any plan for where Clayface goes next? Is he getting ready to fight Robert Pattinson’s Batman or another DC hero?

	That’s a question for James Gunn. I liked the standalone nature of it. I liked how it felt like it introduced a character. But I wasn’t trying to introduce the character to go, “OK, what next?” I was trying to introduce the character as a full meal in itself.

schema.headline: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins Explains That [SPOILER] Cameo, Introducing Gotham City to the DC Universe and All the Shape-Shifting Kills

title: ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ Gets a Fittingly Sexy Fashion Collection Ahead of Sarah J. Maas’s Latest Book
description: In an age of endless brand partnerships and collaborations, it always feels good seeing a team-up that doesn’t feel forced. Such is the case with Fo
body:
In an age of endless brand partnerships and collaborations, it always feels good seeing a team-up that doesn’t feel forced. Such is the case with For Love & Lemons very sexy collaboration with “A Court of Thorns and Roses” — a collection of corsetry, lace, romantic florals and embellished evening wear that just makes sense. 

	The collaboration, which launched Oct. 22, arrives just days before the Oct. 27 release of “A Court of Splintered Harmony,” the sixth installment in Sarah J. Maas’ wildly popular romantasy series. Rather than relying on book-cover graphics and branded sweatshirts, the LA-based brand infused the aesthetic of Maas’ fictional world of Prythian into four mini collections based on themes from the books: “The First Bloom of Spring,” “Welcome to the Night Court,” “Under Starfall Skies” and “A Dance of Silver Flames.”



						
			
	

	
					

	The Spring Court-inspired pieces feature pastel florals and delicate lace, including the $639 Rose of the Manor Gown, while the darker Night Court assortment includes the $629 Night Court Mini Dress and $829 Moonveil Gown. Elsewhere, celestial-inspired Starfall designs and nods to characters like Nesta and the Valkyries round out the collection, with pieces ranging from a $398 beaded mini skirt to a $729 gown.

	“This collection has been over a year in the making, and it was born out of true passion,” For Love & Lemons co-founder Gillian Kern said of the partnership. “We love the way Sarah J. Maas uses fashion to evoke a mood.”

	The collection also includes several pieces featuring custom embroidery, hand-beaded detailing and intricate embellishments. Produced in limited quantities, the designs will not be restocked once sold out, according to the brand. Several styles, including the Storykeeper Dress and Dance with Fire Gown, have already sold out, while other pieces remain listed as coming soon.


	The launch is part of a broader merchandising blitz surrounding the highly anticipated next “ACOTAR” novel. Knix recently debuted a collection of lingerie, sleepwear and underwear inspired by the series, while fragrance brand Fine’ry released four ACOTAR-themed scents. Funko Pop and Loungefly have also rolled out character figurines and accessories, respectively. Meanwhile, Target has launched an extensive assortment of merchandise spanning jewelry, apparel and collectibles, with midnight release celebrations planned at approximately 250 stores on Oct. 26. Barnes & Noble will host similar events at more than 500 locations nationwide.

schema.headline: ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ Gets a Fittingly Sexy Fashion Collection Ahead of Sarah J. Maas’s Latest Book

title: Serielizados Prizes: Hagai Levi’s ‘Etty’ and ‘Astonishing’ ‘Killing a Bear’ Win Big as ‘El Observatorio’ Bags the Mind the Gap Pitch Prize
description: Influential Israeli creator Hagai Levi (“The Affair,” “Scenes From a Marriage”) and prominent Spanish TV-making duo Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabez
body:
Influential Israeli creator Hagai Levi (“The Affair,” “Scenes From a Marriage”) and prominent Spanish TV-making duo Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“La Zona”) won best international and national series at Barcelona’s Serielizados for “Etty” and “Killing a Bear” respectively.

	The prizes for Serielizados two competitive sections were announced Saturday night at a Serielizados awards ceremony.


	Both series in six-parts reflect the boldness of their respective creators, who broke new ground within traditional genres.
	

	In the French-Dutch-German show “Etty,” based on Dutch Jewish author Etty Hillesum’s diaries, Levi deliberately opted for a modern spin to the period piece in which we follow the passionate 27-year-old Etty as she embarks on a spiritual and emotional journey in a Nazi-occupied Amsterdam.

	In the Spanish show “Killing a Bear” (“Matar a un oso”) the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers brought innovation to the crime genre, making a bear the victim, relating the crime from the POV of multiple characters, and expanding the number of prime suspects to a tight community of 262 Anti-Bears chat room in Spain’s idyllic high-Pyrenean Val d’Arán.

	“With this series, we felt really lucky to have been invited into a world so fully realised, so distinctly Catalan but portrayed with a confidence and a muscularity that left us astonished,” said Finnish producer Roosa Toivonen, also Tallinn TV Beats co-head, who sat on the national competition jury with Canneseries’ Claire-Marine Pietriga and the Berlinale’s Rowan Woods.
	



	

					‘Kiling a Bear’
	



	Both series also stand out among the best shows that Europe currently has to offer, with the stamp of approval from quality-maker Arte France.

	Indeed, the European cultural channel was a major backer of Levi’s historical drama – conceived as a feature film in six episodes – which world-premiered out of competition in Venice, was highlighted at Series Mania, and bowed in French cinemas May 6 before launching on Arte.tv on May 16. Shepherded by Les Films du Poisson, “Etty” is sold internationally by Studio TF1.

	“Killing a Bear” which had its Catalan premiered at Serielizados fast on the heels of its world premiere at Spain’s Valladolid Film Festival, is the latest prime example of Arte France’s successful collaboration with the largest Spanish pay-TV/SVOD operator Movistar Plus. The Movistar Plus Original, produced by the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers’ Studio TF1-owned Kubik Films, will bow in Spain Dec. 1.

	Besides the top win for “Etty,” Arte France also scooped best screenplay at Serielizados’ official International Selection Awards for the French comedy “Camarades” co-created and co-penned by Benjamin Charbit (“Under Control”) and Dominique Baumart (“The Bureau”).

	Another comedy wooed the international jury: BBC’s hit show “Ann Droid” for which its creator, Bafta-nominated Diane Morgan (“Mandy,” “Cun”), won best performance for her turn as the second-hand robot Linda.

	On the national competition front, all four selected series won accolades. Next to “Killing a Bear,” the anticipated drama “Segunda Temporada” from the hot creators of Filmin’s “Autodefensa” – writer-director Miguel Ángel Blanca and co-writers Berta Prieto and Víctor Diago – scooped best screenplay. Bringing together a washed-up ghost-writer and a fading trap legend fresh out of jail, the show was developed as part of Serielizados Kick talent lab, before making it as a 7-30-minute drama produced by Barcelona-based Boogaloo Films and Canada. Paris-based Oble handles sales.

	Beloved Spanish-acting queen Carmen Machi (“Aida,” “La Mesías”), bagged a fresh best actress nod for her performance as tax inspector Sara Santano in the Movistar Plus-100 Balas’ “Celeste” Season 2 which bowed as a world premiere in Barcelona. Last year the show’s creator Diego San José and helmer Elena Trapé scooped two Serielizados wins for “Yakarta,” another example of their inimitable downbeat but sharply observant humor.
	

	Elsewhere, the buzzy HBO Max-3Cat co-commissioned dramedy “In Vitro” which offers a witty and heart-warming look at fertility treatments, received a Special Mention. “This [show] really stood out to us for its global appeal and international remake potential,” said the jurors. 

	The series, created by Marc Crehuet with Alejandra Guimerà, was co-penned by Crehuet with Carmen Marfá, Natalia Boadas and Serielizados co-founder Víctor Sala. The latter said the show ,which launched simultaneously Oct. 19 in Spain on HBO Max and 3Cat, garnered an excellent 18.2% share on the Catalan pubcaster.

	“Many countries could be jealous of the creative courage the Spanish commissioners have shown, as they have helped equally bold producers to greenlight shows of this caliber!” said the jurors of the Spanish competition, who highlighted the central female-characters of different ages in each of the four series.

	The jurors added: “Serializados is one of these tremendous gems – smaller events where you can see that the content is lovingly hand-picked and curated out of pure passion for the art and craft of series, and the atmosphere is convivial with a lovely team that truly cares about everyone’s experience and hospitality. We, the jury members, had a great time and watching the four nominated shows was a lot of fun, as they are each so brilliant and original in their very unique ways.”

	Although Serielizados has another few days to run – until Oct. 28 – across various Barcelona venues, co-founder and festival programmer Betu Martínez Molero was pleased with this 13th edition, led by masterclasses with Levi, Steven Moffat and Sue Vertue, a full day of the Miniput -quality TV festival showcase, and the second edition of the Mind the Gap pitch competition.

	Mind the GapThe top €5,500 ($6,100) Mind the Gap Award was handed out to the creators of the Spanish show “El Observatorio,” from Laura Roqué, Luis Sorolla and Eloy Zamora. Set in a small village from Sierra Morena, the story turns on a group of astrophysicists investigating mysterious flickering lights, until one of them-Sara starts to believe the light might be her deceased father trying to communicate.

	“After a great deliberation we’ve decided to award new talent who need to be discovered,” said Arte France’s Alexios Kastrissianakis, co-juror with Mubi’s Ben Driscoll, Movistar Plus’ Laura Escrivá, ZDF Studios’ Susanne Frank and Beta Film’s Peter Lohner. First pitched at the ECAM Forum 2026 where it earned the Serilizados award, the project, in early development, is looking for a producer.
	

	The jury also gave two honorable mentions to two female-led series about abuse: the Finnish psychological drama “Dangerous Woman,” produced by Gutsy Pictures for MTV Finland and TV4 Sweden, and the Spanish drama “Callback” created by sisters Joana and Mireia Vilapuig for “This is Not Sweden” producer Funicular Films, with Left Tackle Films.

	“Callback” was also bestowed the €2,000 ($2,200) Konga Music Agency award.

	Martínez Molero said: “This year we solidified our position as the leading international TV series festival in Spain and one of the most prominent in Southern Europe, reaching 18.000 attendees across more than 60 activities, including more than 30 national and international premieres.” 

	He added: “We’ve seen a growing interest from both media and audiences for our National and International Competitions, packing our main venues. It’s also been great to see how presenting non-distributed international shows helps put them on the radar of Spanish platforms looking to acquire new series, while also helping local creators connect with key international players in the TV industry.”

	Following its onsite showcase in Barcelona, Serielizados will bow on line on the streamer Filmin over Nov. 10-22.

title: Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Forza,” Marco Balsamo’s soccer drama shot between Bali and Milan, has been picked up for international sales by EST N8, which will take the film t
body:
“Forza,” Marco Balsamo’s soccer drama shot between Bali and Milan, has been picked up for international sales by EST N8, which will take the film to the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market (Oct. 28–30). Before that, it gets its first public screening on Oct. 25 at Jakarta Film Week.

	Balsamo’s first feature as director centers on Bima, an 11-year-old from Bali who hopes a career as a pro footballer will give his family a better life. A chance bond with a former AC Milan player in the last stretch of his career changes the outlook for both of them.
	

	Newcomer Ghazi Alhabsyi heads the cast. Balsamo also appears on screen, alongside Tara Sibel Demren, AC Milan icon Alessandro Costacurta and Atiqah Hasiholan, Oka Antara and Tio Pakusadewo, all three winners at the Indonesian Film Festival (FFI).


	Balsamo wrote the script and produced with Demren. Riva Studios originated the project, and its producers include Ario Sagantoro of “The Raid” franchise. Adhya Pictures has the film’s Indonesian theatrical release, set for 2027.

	Interest at home is strong. Both rounds of online tickets for the Jakarta screening, at CGV Grand Indonesia, sold out inside five minutes.

	“‘Forza’ follows a boy from Bali and a former pro footballer who open new doors for each other, and it bridges Indonesia and Italy the way only football can,” said Sophie Shi, head of studios at EST N8. “It’s a film for audiences around the world, with a story of family and hope that transcends language and culture. Our mission is to take bold Asian stories to audiences worldwide, and a family film told through the world’s most popular sport is built to travel. We’re proud to launch ‘Forza’ to buyers at TIFFCOM.”
	

	Shi and Jan Paul Villanueva negotiated the deal for EST N8, with Balsamo and Demren representing Riva Studios. Villanueva, EVP of acquisitions and global distribution, will lead sales with Cathy Ni, head of sales and U.S. distribution, and Shams Pasha, global sales and marketing executive.

	“We’ve spent years bringing ‘Forza’ to the screen, and Indonesia has been at the heart of it from the beginning,” Balsamo said. “This film is a labor of love and a testament to the perseverance and collaboration behind independent filmmaking. Sharing the film at Jakarta Film Week is especially meaningful. It’s a moment we’ve been looking forward to for a long time.”

	Demren, who co-founded Riva Studios, said the film was designed for families to watch side by side and discuss afterward. “We hope Bima’s journey reminds audiences how much it matters to have someone believe in you, especially when your dreams feel out of reach,” she said. “Seeing both ticket releases fill so quickly is an encouraging start. We’re looking forward to hearing audiences’ reactions.”

	Demren and Balsamo set up Riva Studios in 2022 as an independent outfit working in live action, animation and music. In 2024 it bought French animation house TeamTO. “Forza” is its first live-action feature.

	Also on EST N8’s TIFFCOM lineup are “Tame,” a Thai horror title from B-EST Pictures; Dean Colin Marcial’s crime thriller “Jaguar,” set in Manila; “Master,” Rezwan Shahriar Sumit’s winner of IFFR’s Big Screen Award; “Pilgrims,” a Korean sci-fi animation from Heo Pyoungkang that was selected for Annecy; and “The Invisible Half,” a J-horror from Nishiyama Masaki.

	The company, which brought together EST Studios and N8, has offices in Los Angeles and Bangkok and has sold and distributed more than 60 titles across over 100 territories. Its catalog includes “Hidden Letters,” which was shortlisted for the Oscars and nominated for an Emmy; “The Monk and the Gun,” Bhutan’s Oscar entry; “A Useful Ghost,” which won the Grand Prize at Cannes Critics’ Week; and “Blood Brothers,” which topped Netflix’s global chart.

title: Egyptian Cinema Eyes Its Next Act as Industry Veterans Call for Better Scripts, Wider Distribution
description: As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt, the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and fi
body:
As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt, the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and filmmakers turned to what the industry needs to turn its wealth of talent into films that can find audiences both at home and abroad.

	Egyptian cinema once dominated film production across the Arab world, but output fell dramatically from its late-20th-century heights. According to figures from the Egyptian Chamber of Cinema Industry, the country produced 112 films in 1988, before output fell to just 16 a decade later. More recently, production has shown signs of recovery, rising from 51 feature films in 2022 to 67 in 2023.
	

	For veteran Syrian producer Mohamed Mashish, who has built a decades-long career in Egypt, capitalizing on that momentum starts with the screenplay.


	“We need to have more time for development and scriptwriting,” he tells Variety. “We have all the industry components. But we don’t have scripts. So what can you do? I have a nice camera, a good DP, but we can’t do anything without good scripts.”

	Mashish has seen firsthand how new platforms can expand the reach of Egyptian storytelling. He produced the 2016 drama “Grand Hotel,” which became the first Egyptian and first Arabic-language series to land on Netflix when the streamer released it internationally as “Secret of the Nile” in 2018.

	He believes younger filmmakers are also benefiting from greater access to work from around the world. “They’re more open-minded. They’re connected on the internet and everything,” he notes. “Because the platforms are available now, they’re watching more than just our culture. So they are more open and they are ready to move.”
	

	But Mashish argues that new perspectives need to be matched with experience. “We have to bring the old generation and the new generation together,” he explains. “The new generation brings a different perspective, but cinema still needs experience, so we need to combine that new talent with the expertise that already exists in the industry.”

	Egyptian director Hadi El Bagoury, whose 2016 “Hepta: The Last Lecture” became the highest-grossing romantic film in Egyptian cinema, points to streaming as one of the biggest opportunities for homegrown talent.

	The growth of platforms, he argues, has given filmmakers more places to show their work while exposing audiences to a wider range of filmmaking. “You discover new stories, new directors, new genres,” he says. “You discover a lot more directors, DPs, actors and different styles.”

	That exposure is also changing what audiences expect from Egyptian cinema. “They want new genres, they want original stories,” El Bagoury says.

	The shift has particular consequences in the Gulf, a crucial market for Egyptian films. Mashish points to Saudi Arabia’s theatrical expansion as an example of how quickly audiences have evolved.

	“At the beginning, when the Saudis started to open cinemas, they accepted everything because it was new,” he recalls. “It’s like, ‘I will go to the cinema, I will have popcorn, no matter the kind of movie I will watch.'”

	“They are more selective than before,” he continues. “They will not accept just anything coming anymore. Because cinemas are now open in Saudi and in the Gulf, they are watching international cinema. So they demand this kind of quality.”

	For Lebanese producer and distributor Ziad Srouji (“Palestine 36”), whose career spans film and television across the Arab world, reaching audiences beyond the region does not mean making Arab films resemble foreign ones.

	“Specificity travels; generic does not,” he stresses. “International buyers aren’t looking for Arab films that imitate Western genre cinema, and they’re tired of films made only to explain the region to outsiders. They want stories rooted in a very particular world but driven by a premise anyone can grasp in one sentence.”

	For Srouji, the challenges often come after the initial idea. “A good idea gets you into the room. It doesn’t get you through production, and it certainly doesn’t get you to an audience.”
	

	The bigger obstacles, he believes, are often structural. “Too many films reach the market without a sales agent attached early, without delivery materials ready and without a positioning strategy beyond a festival premiere,” Srouji says. “Sales and distribution need a strategy built from day one, not after the premiere.”

	El Gouna is among the regional festivals trying to strengthen the path from development onward. CineGouna, its industry arm, launched the Egyptian Voices strand this year, selecting four Egyptian projects in development for tailored training in pitching, packaging and co-production.

	El Bagoury argues that the industry also needs more ways to reach audiences directly. “We need more Egyptian-owned platforms, more theaters. Theaters that are cheap, accessible to all,” he says. “We need a lot of this so we don’t have to depend on anybody else. We need to show our films in our cinemas and on our platforms.”

	For Srouji, the ultimate measure of a healthy industry is not simply whether a filmmaker gets a movie made or lands a prestigious festival selection, but whether that success makes the next film possible.

	“A major festival selection is a launch, not a career,” he says. “Sustainable success is when your second film is easier to finance than your first.”

title: Jay-Z Brings His ‘Jay-Z 30’ Concert Series to a Close in Los Angeles With Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short
description: How does one measure their own legacy: In a series of shows, in the decades since a debut album, in an exhaustive eight-part docuseries breaking do
body:
How does one measure their own legacy: In a series of shows, in the decades since a debut album, in an exhaustive eight-part docuseries breaking down the intricacies of rhymes laid down years ago? That seemed to be the existential question looming over “Jay-Z 30,” a yearlong celebration that began with a spectacular one-off headlining performance at the Roots Picnic in late May and concluded on Saturday night with the second of two shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium.
	

	For Jay, legacy has clearly been weighing on his mind. A new generation of hip-hop artists has emerged, and the decade-long gap since he released an album has opened a space for that generation to question his legacy. So it made sense that he’d revisit his catalog brick by brick, show by show, celebrating a career-long work in progress that crescendoed to a global tour after nearly a decade of artistic dormancy. At SoFi, much like his previous concerts, his performance was a reminder — no, a reinforcement — that nothing at that scale is by accident. And he said as much as the curtain fell on an hour-and-a-half finale of his “Jay-Z 30” series, encouraging those in attendance to believe in what they’ve actually witnessed.


	“You gotta be really real with what’s going on in the world,” he said during closer “Encore.” It was a direct rebuttal to the rash of tweets and social media posts claiming that SoFi wasn’t entirely sold out, or that many of the tickets had been given away. “People will tell you that nobody was in here tonight, but you got eyes. You can see. People will tell you that the music wasn’t great, but you got ears. You gotta understand, you gotta question everything. This world with AI and everything, it’s been going on forever. They called it propaganda before. But now, the technology has caught up and people are tricked. A lot of tricknology for us… Make sure you question everything you feel.”
	


	Jay makes that music that you can feel. That’s been the thrill of his shows over the past five months. For those who experienced his rise in real time (and, frankly, many at SoFi probably had, based on their millennial look), Jay has been a pop impresario, a cultural touchstone who helped graft hip-hop culture onto the mainstream. He’s done it through a breathless string of number one albums and hits, and in boardrooms and closed-door meetings. “Jay-Z 30” was an invitation to revisit the path that he took to get there, a way to show that legacy isn’t about the hit that’s next, but rather the ones you landed to get there.

	To witness it was where the details mattered most. Much like his other performances, the setlist at Jay’s final night at SoFi was somewhat static — “Girls, Girls, Girls,” for instance, once again bled into “’03 Bonnie & Clyde,” while “N—s in Paris” delightfully mashed into “Big Pimpin’.” But the finer details are what make a Jay show such an experience. At each of his shows, he’s found a way to pay homage to the city that’s welcomed him. In Philadelphia, that included guest appearances from Jazmine Sullivan, Bilal and his Roc-A-Fella crew, including Freeway, Beanie Sigel and Peedi Crakk. In New York City, throughout his three-night run at Yankee Stadium, he brought out Alicia Keys for “Empire State of Mind,” as well as Fat Joe and Jadakiss. Naturally, a narrative emerged: Can he really perform a solid headlining set without a supporting cast to sweeten the deal?

	Perhaps that’s why the guest count at his SoFi shows was so thin compared to others. On Saturday night, he tapped Too Short to perform “Blow the Whistle,” shouting out the Bay Area. Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg came out to do a medley of their own massive hits, including “Nuthin’ But a ‘G’ Thang” and “Still D.R.E.” But it was mainly Jay, every day, in all his resplendence. He traipsed from era to era, hit to hit, his breath control and spark as refined as ever. This was performance at its peak, a marvel to behold of an artist who helped build hip-hop as an institution while adding to the story still being written.


	As for what’s next? Rumors have swirled about a new album from collaborators who quickly backpedaled on their statements. The looming question mark of a Super Bowl Halftime Show performance hung in the air at SoFi on Saturday night. But for a string of concerts and a few activations here and there, it felt only right that Jay-Z justify the experience while rapping “Heart of the City (Ain’t No Love)” near the end of the show: “Jigga held you down 30 summers, damn, where’s the love?”
	

	Check out the full setlist below:

title: ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2
description: Stars of “Squid Game” and “KPop Demon Hunters” took the stage in Seoul on Oct. 24 as Netflix celebrated 10 years in Korea with a fan festival, wher
body:
Stars of “Squid Game” and “KPop Demon Hunters” took the stage in Seoul on Oct. 24 as Netflix celebrated 10 years in Korea with a fan festival, where co-CEO Ted Sarandos previewed upcoming titles including “Tantara” and “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2.

	“Squid Game” was represented by Lee Jung-jae, Lee Byung-hun and Park Hae-soo, while Ahn Hyo-seop appeared for “KPop Demon Hunters.” Also on stage were Koo Kyo-hwan and Jung Hae-in of “D.P.,” Kim Hyun-joo of “Hellbound,” Yum Hye-ran of “Mask Girl” and Lee Se-dol of “The Devil’s Plan,” among others.
	

	Dubbed “Netflix Janchi,” the two-day event ran Oct. 24-25 at Sangam Oil Tank Culture Park. Thousands of fans turned out for themed booths, games, merchandise and live music.


	“Ten years ago, we dreamed big. But none of us could have imagined that Korean stories would move hearts around the world, and land right at the center of global culture,” Sarandos said.

	Of the new titles, Lee Chang-dong’s Venice winner “Possible Love,” headlined by Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Cho Yeo-jeong and Jo In-sung, bows Nov. 6. “Tantara,” starring Song Hye-kyo, Gong Yoo and Kim Seol-hyun, follows on Dec. 11. Still undated are “Grand Galaxy Hotel,” with Lee Do-hyun and Shin Si-a; “She, Wolf,” previously known by the working title “Beauty in the Beast,” with Kim Min-ju, Lomon and Moon Sang-min; “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2, with Park Ji-hu, Yoon Chan-young, Cho Yi-hyun and Lomon; and “Solo Leveling,” with Byeon Woo-seok.

	Netflix launched in Korea on Jan. 6, 2016. Its first international film was Bong Joon Ho’s “Okja.” The first Korean original, the stand-up special “Yoo Byung Jae: Too Much Information,” arrived in March 2018, and “Kingdom” became its first Korean series in January 2019. In July 2021, “Kingdom: Ashin of the North” became the first Korean show to crack the Global Top 10, charting in 58 countries.
	

	Netflix has counted upward of 200 Korean titles on its Global Top 10 since it began compiling the chart in June 2021. “Squid Game” Season 1 holds the record for the longest run at 32 straight weeks, nine of them at No. 1. The show’s three seasons are the streamer’s three most-watched non-English series ever, and “Teach You a Lesson” now ranks No. 10 on that list, making it Netflix’s biggest Korean show after “Squid Game.” No other non-English content draws more viewing on Netflix than K-content, and over four in five of its subscribers worldwide have sampled at least one Korean title.

	“For Netflix, Korea is more than a market. It is where we discovered new possibilities, and where we learned how far a story can travel. And it is one of our most treasured partners for the future we are building together,” Sarandos said.

	Between 2024 and 2026, first-time directors or writers made more than a third of Netflix’s Korean titles. Park Yoon-seo, an assistant director on “Kingdom” Season 2, made his directing debut this year with YA horror series “If Wishes Could Kill.”

	“Netflix gave me an opportunity when I was an assistant director on ‘Kingdom: Season 2.’ I’m glad I was able to give new actors that same opportunity,” Park said. He added that he had suggested casting only newcomers to keep the series fresh, and that Netflix signed off because fame wasn’t the priority.

	Baek Seung-min was a second lighting assistant on “Kingdom” and now heads lighting on “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2. “Working with Netflix Korea at important stages of my career has helped me grow professionally,” he said.

	From 2016 to 2025, Netflix partnered with more than 80 Korean production companies on shows employing upward of 20,000 actors and crew members, along with 70,000 extras and day workers. Shoots took place in more than 100 cities and towns, with over half outside the Seoul Capital Area in locations such as Busan, Jeonju and Jeju. “When Life Gives You Tangerines” alone drew on nearly 4,000 suppliers and a cast and crew of 600, adding more than KRW90 billion ($60.4 million) to the Korean economy. Netflix’s skills and training programs reached over 6,500 people in Korea between 2021 and 2025.

	To get those shows to viewers abroad, Netflix now relies on 122 localization partners globally, 119 of them dubbing studios.
	

	Colorist Park Jin-young, whose credits include “Possible Love” and “Good News,” said Netflix’s arrival in Korea came just as HDR technology was going commercial. “It felt like going from working with 30 colors of paint for 10 or 20 years to suddenly having 100 colors at my disposal,” he said.

	Unscripted formats have also exported well. “Physical: 100” became the first unscripted show not in English to lead the Global Top 10, and local versions have followed in Italy and Mexico, with U.S., French and Swedish editions on the way.

	The streamer also pointed to effects off screen. According to Netflix, 72% of subscribers who watch K-content have said they’d like to travel to Korea. Jeju drew about 2.24 million overseas visitors in 2025, its most in nine years, coinciding with the premiere of “When Life Gives You Tangerines,” while visits to the show’s Gimnyeong Beach location jumped about 96%. Chef Choi Hyun-seok’s restaurant Choi saw sales rise 300% after “Culinary Class Wars” Season 1, and bookings at restaurants of Season 2 contestants climbed 303%.

	In the U.S., new Korean learners on Duolingo rose 37% in the week “Squid Game” Season 3 launched. Applications for Korea’s TOPIK language exam passed 550,000 in September 2025, three months on from “KPop Demon Hunters,” beating the total for all of 2024. Between April 2025 and March 2026, K-content logged more than 12 billion viewing hours on Netflix, behind only U.S. productions, and rights to the “Hellbound” webtoon have sold to 11 countries since the series launched.

	Netflix has also opened a Korean-language microsite charting the people, locations and numbers behind its first decade in the country.

Prostitution Scam Case
                          Teacher Accused of Holding Naked Man Down, Sending $1K in Apple Pay: Report
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A New Jersey middle school teacher has been accused of running a prostitution scam that involved her allegedly pinning down a naked man ... but she claims she was "strictly there to party."
      
    
            An unidentified man claims he met Middle Township Middle School computer teacher Amanda Crafts, 35, and Veda Engel, 23, at Caesar’s Atlantic City on Oct. 9 ... the New York Post reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The victim claims that after Engel performed a sex act on him in the women's Harrah's hotel room ... Crafts held him down and used his smartphone's Face ID to open up Apple Pay to send 4 separate payments totaling $1,250.
      

            Craft's legal team has denied her involvement in pinning the man down ... and rejected the claim that she knew Engel was a prostitute.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Crafts' attorney told the NYP ... "Amanda Crafts is highly intelligent and wouldn’t participate in anything like that. She was in the room and wanted to leave and didn’t even realize it was a prostitution thing. She is mortified."
      
    
            Since her arrest on Oct. 9 and release on Oct. 15 ... Crafts is out of a job.
      
    
            Middle Township Middle School announced in a letter on Oct. 19 to parents and fellow staffers that she was "no longer employed by the district."
      
    
            Craft faces 2 charges connected to the alleged prostitution scam.

                            7:18 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The NFL has confirmed they're launching an investigation into Jalen Hurts' medical care and blood clot diagnosis ... after the player was sidelined for the rest of the season.
      
    
            The league confirmed the probe into about how the Philadelphia Eagles handled the diagnosis in a joint statement with the National Football League Players Association Sunday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Their statement reads ... "The NFL and NFL Players Association are working together to review the matter."
      

            The investigation comes after the NFLPA demanded a full inquiry be made by the league into how his medical treatment was handled.
      
    
            They wrote last week ... "Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."
      
    
            As you know ... Hurts was initially diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his leg ... before the clot spread to his lungs where multiple clots were found.
      
    
            Hurts is now out for the remainder of the season ... and based on what we're hearing, it's imperative he stay off the field.
      
    
            Doctor David Abbasi told Jakson on TMZ's "In The Know" ... the star athlete could be out for 3 to 6 months due to the risk of incurring serious damage from bleeding.
